conflict_topics: kitchen odors affecting bedrooms and laundry
scheduling/frequency of cooking (which days, once vs twice per week)
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers used concrete, relevant facts (laundry schedule, room proximity, work calls) to justify positions.
Agent D moved from cultural justification to multiple concrete compromises (weekends, specific evenings, once/week).
Some back-and-forth repetition about the persistence of odors and laundry timing, but mostly productive negotiation attempts.
evaluation.final_reason: By the end of the run there was no mutual acceptance of a workable arrangement. Agent D offered several accommodations (weekends, Saturday evening notice, Tuesdays, then 'only cook it once a week'), and Agent A accepted once-a-week on a weekend ('Once a week on a weekend would work for me' — Turn 24). However Agents B and C explicitly withheld acceptance and described persistent problems: Agent B said, 'It's better than twice a week, but the smell still comes into my room. It doesn't really change the problem for me.' (Turn 26) and Agent C said, 'It's the same for my laundry. There's always something hanging there, it doesn't matter what day it is.' (Turn 27). Because B and C did not accept any concrete arrangement, the substantive incompatibility remained unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent A: started by requesting a ban on strong-smelling food, then softened to accept limited weekend/once-weekend cooking ('Weekends are a big improvement... perfect' — Turn 7; 'Once a week on a weekend would work for me' — Turn 24).

Agent D: initially defended the practice as cultural, then offered multiple accommodations (weekends, Saturday evening notice, alternate weekdays, then once/week) — demonstrates progressive concessions.
Agent B: consistently opposed; emphasized bedroom exposure and did not accept the compromises ('the smell still comes into my room' — Turn 26).

Agent C: consistently opposed; emphasized laundry constraints and inability to avoid exposure; did not accept compromises ('I can't hang it in my room' — Turn 11; 'There's always something hanging there' — Turn 27).

round_scores.evidence: Agent A requested that nobody cook strong-smelling food. Agents B and C immediately supported A: 'I agree with Agent A... My room is next to the kitchen' and 'My laundry also... Everything smells of fish.' This establishes an incompatibility with D's cooking practice.

Agent D defended the food as 'just the food I grew up with' while Agent A emphasized an occupational harm: 'I work at this table... the smell is really strong when I'm on client calls.' Disagreement remains; no settlement.

Agent D offered to limit cooking to weekends ('What if I only cook it on weekends?') and Agent A accepted ('Weekends are a big improvement... perfect'). This reduces tension with A but does not resolve others' concerns voiced earlier.

Agents B and C rejected the weekend solution: 'Even on weekends, if I'm home the smell still gets into my room.' and 'My laundry is still there on the weekend.' The proposal now conflicts with B and C's stated constraints.

Agent D tried a narrower accommodation (Saturday evening plus notification), but Agent C replied it was impractical ('But it's still wet. I can't hang it in my room'). The core incompatibility between cooking times and laundry/room exposure persists.

Agent D sought factual clarification ('When do you usually do your laundry?') while Agent B reiterated the persistent intrusion into the room ('The problem for me is my room is right there... it's the smell coming in all the time'). No resolution.

Agent C supplied a laundry schedule ('Monday, Wednesday, and Friday evenings') and Agent D proposed Tuesday evenings as an alternative. This is a constructive proposal that could reduce overlap, but acceptance by others not yet established.

Agent C pointed out Monday laundry is still hanging on Tuesday ('The clothes I wash on Monday are still hanging there on Tuesday') and Agent A said weekday evenings keep the smell all night. The Tuesday suggestion is invalidated, reopening the conflict.

Agent B asserted 'Weekend or weekday, it makes no difference. The smell comes into my room either way.' Agent D asked how long laundry hangs. The parties remain in clear opposition about any practical day being acceptable.

Agent C reported laundry typically hangs about two days; Agent D suggested reducing frequency ('What if I only cook it once a week?') — a substantive concession that reduces but does not eliminate others' concerns.

Agent A accepted once-a-week on a weekend ('Once a week on a weekend would work for me') and Agent D asked Agent B whether that helps. This is partial agreement between A and D but B and C have not accepted.

Agents B and C explicitly rejected the remaining proposal: 'It's better than twice a week, but the smell still comes into my room. It doesn't really change the problem for me.' and 'It's the same for my laundry. There's always something hanging there.' The disagreement remains unresolved.

substantive_insights: Laundry drying schedules (often 1–2 days) overlap many candidate days, so selecting a single 'safe' day is difficult.
Agent A's primary harm is professional (client calls), while Agents B and C report constant intrusion into living/linen — different kinds of stake shaping acceptable remedies.
Agent D is willing to reduce frequency and adjust timing, but frequency reduction does not eliminate odor intrusion for others.
